newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade minister a lawmaker of elite pedigree.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade minister a lawmaker of elite pedigree.

text.p: Japan's new trade minister, Shinji Sato, is a veteran lawmaker with an elite political pedigree.
The son of former prime minister Eisaku Sato, Japan's longest-ruling prime minister in the post-war period, Sato also has a modicum of experience when it comes to trade matters.
The 64-year-old Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) parliamentarian, who served as transport minister in 1988, has also held the post of parliamentary vice minister of trade.

Sato, a member of one of the LDP's biggest factions, worked behind the scenes with other powerful lawmakers to put Ryutaro Hashimoto in the prime minister's seat in January, an effort which helped boost his influence in the party.

Aides say that unlike his father, a Nobel Peace prize laureate known for his reserved manner, Sato's experience at a major Japanese steel maker before entering politics in 1979 makes him a more approachable character.
While his predecessors have often had to engage in tough tete-a-tete talks in trade spats, Sato takes over at a time when many thorny issues have moved to the multilateral arena.

High on his ministry's agenda are two cases now pending at the Geneva-based World Trade Organisation (WTO) -- complaints by Japan and the United States over Indonesia's national car project and U.S. allegations of barriers in Japan's consumer photo film market.

Japan and the United States earlier this year complained to the world trade body about Indonesia's controversial car policy, arguing that the scheme in which domestic car makers enjoy tax and tariff breaks violated WTO rules and discriminated against foreign manufacturers.

The United States, meanwhile, has taken to the WTO its complaints over limited access to Japan's consumer photo film and paper market. Japan says it will honour any WTO verdict, which may not be reached until late next year or early 1998.
Sato's debut on the world trade stage is likely to be at a meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum later this month in the Philippines.
He also heads a friendship committee of Japanese and Taiwanese parliamentarians, making him a potential pipeline on simmering territorial issues between Tokyo and Taipei.
